newsitem.title: USA: U.S. West spot electricity prices largely flat.
newsitem.headline: U.S. West spot electricity prices largely flat.

text.p: Spot power prices in the U.S. West were largely flat amid forecasts for cooler temperatures in both the Northwest and Southwest, transmission constraints and a potential for lower hydroelectric dam flows, trade sources said Tuesday.
"Buyers in the Southwest are trapped in (because of the planned DC intertie outage). They have to get power from within the Southwest," said one trader.
But cool temperatures in the Southwest have reduced the impact of the outage, he and others noted.
As scheduled, transmissions on the 3,200-megawatt (MW) DC segment of the Pacific Intertie are cut to zero from 0600 PDT Tuesday through 2000 PDT on Sunday due to system maintenance.
After Sunday, the north to south transmissions DC line will be limited until further notice to 2,000 MW during heavy-load hours and to 2,200 MW during light-load hours.
Next-day Palo Verde power was last quoted at $19.00-20.00, little changed from $19.25-19.75 on Monday.
California-Oregon border (COB) next-day was last quoted at $19.25-19.50, up from $19.00-19.25.
MidColumbia was last quoted at $17.25-17.75, unchanged from Monday.
Under the "Vernita Bar" requirements, daytime dam flows between now and mid-November become a benchmark minimum for the remainder of the winter so that fish nests do not dry out.
The Bonneville Power Administration, which markets power produced from federal dams in the region, said the target for flows during this period is 50,000 to 70,000 cubic feet per second.
Cash November prices for COB were last quoted $17.20-$17.40, while Palo Verde was at $16.65-16.80 and MidColumiba was quoted 16.50-16.90.
